html:
Jean-Jacques Rousseau was a philosopher and writer born in Geneva in 1712. He signed himself Citizen of Geneva, though he lived mostly in France.

In The Social Contract of 1762 he argued that a legitimate state rests on the general will of its citizens, a model drawn partly from his idea of the Genevan republic. Emile set out a new way of raising children. His novel Julie and his Confessions helped start the Romantic cult of feeling and nature.

Geneva burned The Social Contract and Emile in 1762. Rousseau spent years in flight. After his death the leaders of the French Revolution treated him as a prophet and moved his remains to the Pantheon. He was a key figure of the Enlightenment, and a sharp critic of it, alongside Voltaire.
